explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Why does the training corpus become a list of (word, count) pairs before BPE starts?
options: Because BPE only works on English
Because the end-of-word marker requires it
Because it removes rare words
Because pairs are never counted across word boundaries, so identical words can be processed once and weighted by their count
explain: Sennrich et al. do not count pairs that cross word boundaries. Then every occurrence of the same word behaves identically, so the algorithm can run on the word dictionary with each word weighted by its frequency, which is far faster than scanning the raw text each step.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
question: A completion prompt ends with "The answer is " (trailing space) and the model's answers often look odd. Which change addresses the tokenizer cause?
options: Raise the sampling temperature
Remove the trailing space, so the model can produce the space together with the next word, or use token healing
Add more examples before the question
Switch to a tokenizer with a larger vocabulary
explain: Words usually carry their leading space inside their token. Ending the prompt with a bare space forces a lone-space token followed by a no-space word, a pattern rare in training. Dropping the space, or backing up one token and constraining the next one (token healing), puts the model back on familiar token boundaries.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
question: A 56-layer plain network ends training with higher *training* error than a 20-layer one built the same way. What does that tell you?
options: It is overfitting, so it needs more regularization
The deeper net is harder to optimize: a solution as good as the 20-layer one exists, but SGD does not find it
The 56-layer net has too few parameters to fit the data
The test set is too small to compare the two
explain: Overfitting lowers training error and raises test error. Higher training error despite more capacity is an optimization failure: copying the 20-layer net and adding identity layers would match it. Residual connections make that identity solution easy to reach.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Mixed precision: fp16, bf16 and loss scaling
question: Roughly how much memory do the weights, gradients and Adam state of a 7-billion-parameter model need in mixed precision training, before activations?
options: 14 GB
28 GB
112 GB
56 GB
explain: 16 bytes per parameter: fp16 weights and gradients (2 + 2) plus fp32 master weights, m and v (4 + 4 + 4). 16 x 7e9 = 112e9 bytes. Only the fp16 weights alone would be 14 GB.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: Which logged signal most directly catches a scheduler, written for per-step use, being stepped only once per epoch?
options: The global gradient norm
The dead ReLU fraction
The learning rate itself
The last layer's activation std
explain: The other signals change only indirectly and slowly. The logged learning rate shows immediately that warmup is crawling or the decay is far too slow.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Production scale: disk, rescoring, filters and updates
question: 200 million 768-d vectors, one machine with 64 GB of RAM and a fast SSD. 10 percent of queries carry a tenant filter that matches 0.5 percent of rows (1 million vectors). Which design fits?
options: HNSW over float32 vectors in RAM, post-filtering tenant queries with ef_search = 40
IVF with nprobe = 1 and no re-ranking, post-filtering tenant queries
An SSD-resident graph with 96-byte PQ codes in RAM (about 19 GB) and re-ranking from SSD, plus a separate index per tenant (partitioning) for filtered queries
Binary codes (96 bytes per vector) with no rescoring, post-filtering tenant queries
explain: Float32 vectors alone are 614 GB, so in-RAM HNSW cannot fit. 96-byte PQ codes take about 19 GB, and DiskANN-style search re-ranks from SSD. A 0.5 percent filter leaves post-filtering with about 40 x 0.005 = 0.2 rows, and brute force over 1 million 768-d rows reads about 3 GB per query, so a per-tenant index is the bounded option (even scanning its PQ codes is a million per query). Unrescored binary codes and nprobe = 1 give up too much recall.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: A team uses `pip install --extra-index-url <private>` and their internal package is version 3.2.0. An attacker publishes the same name on PyPI as 3.1.9. What does pip install?
options: Both versions side by side
Nothing; pip errors on duplicate names
3.1.9, because PyPI is the main index
3.2.0, because it is the best match across all indexes
explain: No index has priority and the highest matching version wins, so here the private 3.2.0 wins. The attack only works when the attacker picks a higher number, which is why Birsan used high versions. The design flaw remains: whoever publishes the highest number decides.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: A pipeline needs to publish a package. Which setup leaves the least for a Codecov-style script to steal?
options: The token hard-coded in the workflow file
The token only in the publish job, as an environment variable
OIDC trusted publishing in a dedicated publish job that runs no third-party tools
A long-lived registry token stored as a repository secret, available to all jobs
explain: With OIDC there is no stored token at all; the short-lived credential is minted for that job and expires. Isolating the publish job keeps third-party code away from it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
question: Which question can an SBOM answer on its own?
options: Is any component in this product malicious?
Which of our products contain ms version 2.1.3, and through which dependency path?
Is the vulnerable function actually called?
Was the build server compromised?
explain: Inventory and relationships are exactly what an SBOM records. Maliciousness, build integrity and reachability need other data: advisories, provenance and code analysis.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
question: A developer's laptop installed axios 1.14.1 at 01:10 UTC on 31 March 2026. They have since upgraded to 1.15.0. What is the correct next step?
options: Run npm audit and close the ticket if it is clean
Delete node_modules and reinstall
Treat the laptop as compromised: rotate every credential it held from another machine, investigate it, and rebuild it
Nothing: the upgrade removed the malicious code
explain: The postinstall dropper installed a separate remote access trojan and erased its traces. The axios post-mortem says to treat the machine as compromised and rotate every secret, token and credential on it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
question: Why does the x86-64 Linux syscall convention pass the 4th argument in r10 instead of rcx, which the normal C calling convention uses?
options: The syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the user return address
The kernel needs rcx to hold the syscall number
r10 is faster to read from kernel mode
rcx is reserved for the error code
explain: The `syscall` instruction saves the return address in rcx and rflags in r11, so anything you put in rcx is destroyed by the instruction itself. The kernel's entry comment notes that arg3 arrives in r10 and must be moved to rcx to match the C ABI before calling C handlers.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
question: Why does fan-out make tail latency matter more than median latency for the user?
options: Because the root averages the leaf latencies, and averages are dominated by outliers
Because leaves process requests serially
Because the user waits for the slowest of N responses, so a rare per-leaf event becomes a common per-request event
Because median latency cannot be measured at the root
explain: The root waits for the maximum, not the mean, of the leaf latencies. The probability that the maximum includes a tail event grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR
question: A partner network sends your HLR a request about IMSI 234150999999999. Your network is MCC 234, MNC 15. What does the IMSI tell your HLR?
options: Nothing: an IMSI is just a random serial number
Which country the subscriber is in right now
That the subscriber is yours, because the MCC and MNC name your network as home
The subscriber's phone number
explain: The MCC and MNC at the start of an IMSI identify the home network (TS 23.003). They say nothing about where the phone is now (that is the HLR's location record), and the phone number is the separate MSISDN.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
question: Why is checking Origin-Realm alone not enough?
options: Origin-Realm is encrypted and cannot be read
Origin-Realm only exists in SS7
Realms change every hour
Origin-Realm is written by the sender, so it must be bound to the authenticated peer or connection the message actually came from
explain: The field is a claim. Without binding it to the transport peer, a rogue sender with interconnect access simply writes a partner's realm. 5G makes this binding explicit at the SEPP.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM and eSIM: the key in your pocket, and how it gets there
question: Why could Simjacker work on phones from almost every manufacturer?
options: All those phones ran the same operating system version
It exploited a bug in the radio chipset of every phone
It used SS7 to change each phone's firmware
The vulnerable software was the S@T Browser on the SIM card, and phones passed the SMS to the card
explain: CERT-EU notes the attack depends on software on the UICC, not the device. Handsets forward such messages to the card, so the brand of phone did not matter; that is also why the fix sat with operators and card settings.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Satellite links: segments, footprints and cleartext GEO traffic
question: Why can one receiving station observe traffic meant for terminals hundreds of kilometres away?
options: A GEO transponder's forward link is broadcast across a footprint that can cover a third of Earth, so any dish inside it can receive the signal
Satellites forward every packet to every country on purpose
The researchers hacked the satellites
Terminals send copies of their traffic to anyone who asks
explain: The study was passive: it received broadcasts. GEO footprints are huge by design, which is why confidentiality has to come from encryption, not from location.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a telecom and space defence map
question: Which pair of controls addresses the same underlying problem in two generations of signalling?
options: SMS home routing and Galileo OSNMA
SUCI and router golden configs
Satellite IPsec and carrier account locks
SS7 category 2 filtering and the 5G SEPP's check of the originating network ID against the peer's certificate
explain: Both decide whether the sender may speak about this subscriber or network. Category 2 filtering compares the sender's GT with the IMSI's home; the SEPP compares the claimed network ID with what the authenticated peer's certificate represents, which closes the spoofing gap.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: Which pair of toy roles is in the relation *finishes*?
options: B finishes A
C finishes D
E finishes D
A finishes C
explain: E (Mar 2024 to Present) and D (Sep 2021 to Present) end at the same point and E starts later, so E finishes D. B is during A, A is before C, and C overlaps or precedes D depending on the convention.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
question: A verifier has true positive rate 0.95 and false positive rate 0.02. On a problem where 2% of samples are correct, what accuracy does best-of-N approach as N grows?
options: About 0.95, its true positive rate
About 0.98, one minus its false positive rate
About 1.0, because coverage reaches 1
About 0.49
explain: The ceiling is $pt / (pt + (1-p)f) = 0.019 / (0.019 + 0.0196) = 0.49$. Correct accepted samples and wrong accepted samples arrive at almost the same rate because wrong samples outnumber correct ones 49 to 1.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention. Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression predicts a weighted average of stored values, weighted by a kernel's similarity between the query and each stored key.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In Titans (MAC) at test time, which part keeps changing its weights as the input streams in?
options: The persistent memory tokens
The attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V
All three, since Titans fine-tunes itself at test time
The neural long-term memory M
explain: The paper is explicit: persistent memory parameters stay fixed because they encode task knowledge, the attention weights are fixed in-context learners, and only the long-term memory keeps learning (memorizing) at test time.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: Stacking scheduled task names across all machines gives 4,800 values that each appear once. What most likely went wrong?
options: The query needs a longer time range
Stacking does not work on scheduled tasks
The key contains a variable part (for example a user name or GUID) that should be normalised first
The fleet is heavily compromised
explain: A long tail made of thousands of singletons usually means the values differ only in an irrelevant part. Replace the variable part with a placeholder and stack again; the real outliers then stand out from a short tail.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
question: Host A's connection gaps to one address have a mean of 300 seconds and a standard deviation of 3 seconds. Host B's have a mean of 300 and a standard deviation of 240. Which is more likely automated check-ins, and what is each CV?
options: A: CV 0.01; B: CV 0.8. A is machine-like
Both are identical because the means are equal
B: CV 0.8 is more regular than A
explain: CV = standard deviation / mean: 3 / 300 = 0.01 for A and 240 / 300 = 0.8 for B. A connects almost exactly every five minutes, which is how scheduled software (benign or malicious) behaves. B varies like human activity. Next step for A: which process makes the connection, and is the destination rare?

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt is disproven: no ntds.dit copies on any domain controller in 90 days. What belongs in its write-up?
options: A statement that the network is secure
The hypothesis, data and time range checked, queries used, known-benign ntdsutil uses by named admins, any gaps found, and the detection or baseline it produced
Only the queries
Nothing; disproven hunts are not documented
explain: A disproven hunt is evidence that one behaviour did not occur in the data you had, for the period you checked. Writing down exactly what was checked, what was benign and what was missing lets the next hunter build on it, and keeps anyone from overstating it as 'the network is secure'.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
question: A partner CERT (computer emergency response team) with a long record of accurate reporting shares a claim that no one else has reported and that fits what you already know. What grade fits best?
options: A1
F2
B5
A2
explain: The source has a history of complete reliability (A). The claim is logical and consistent but not independently confirmed, which is 2 (probably true), not 1. F would ignore the track record, and 5 would mean the claim is contradicted.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph
question: You have linked twelve intrusions by shared tooling and infrastructure but have no idea who is behind them. Which STIX object fits the cluster?
options: Threat Actor
Identity
Observed Data
Intrusion Set
explain: STIX defines an Intrusion Set as grouped adversarial behaviours and resources believed to be orchestrated by a single organisation, and allows activity to be attributed to it even when the Threat Actors are not known. A Threat Actor object asserts actual individuals or organisations.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Reading an intelligence product: CISA AA24-038A on Volt Typhoon
question: AA24-038A says conventional IOCs are 'generally lacking' for Volt Typhoon. What is the main reason?
options: The agencies chose not to publish indicators
The malware deletes itself after exactly 24 hours
IOCs are illegal to share across borders
The actors use built-in system tools, valid accounts and proxy networks of ordinary home and office routers, leaving few unique artefacts
explain: Living off the land means using tools already on the system and legitimate accounts, and the KV botnet routers give ordinary-looking source addresses. There is little malware to hash and little stable infrastructure to block, so behaviour detection and hunting carry the load.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Drawing the system: data flow diagrams and trust boundaries
question: A request travels from the Notes API to the database on another host inside your private network. Is that flow across a trust boundary?
options: No, because both are on the private network
No, because the API wrote the query itself
Usually yes: trust level changes between the app and data tiers, so the database should authenticate and limit the API
Only if the traffic is unencrypted
explain: A boundary is wherever the level of trust changes, not only the internet edge. Being on the same network is a location, not a trust decision. Encryption protects the flow but does not decide whether a boundary exists.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
question: Two threats score 10 x 1 and 1 x 10 on probability times damage. What does that tell you?
options: They are equally urgent
Very little on its own: a frequent nuisance and a rare disaster look identical, so you need the reasons behind the scores
The first should be fixed first because it is more likely
The scoring was done wrong
explain: The Microsoft guide shows exactly this example to illustrate how the product works. Equal scores do not mean equal decisions; the reasons and the kind of harm matter.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Defence in depth and zero trust
question: Layers A, B and C each miss 20% of attacks independently. All three share one admin account that, if stolen, disables them all, with a 5% chance per year. Roughly what is the yearly chance of getting through?
options: About 5.8%
explain: Independent part: 0.2 cubed = 0.008. With the shared failure: 0.05 + 0.95 x 0.008 = 0.0576, about 5.8%. The shared account dominates; removing it matters more than a fourth layer.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: Why does the kernel compute a single *top tier* boundary instead of letting every node promote to any faster node?
options: Because pages can only migrate between nodes in adjacent tiers
Because sysfs can only show one tier
Because the top tier is always exactly one node
Because memory near CPUs is where hot pages should end up; promoting between DRAM nodes is NUMA balancing's normal job, not tiering
explain: Tier promotion moves hot pages out of slow, CPU-less memory into memory that has CPUs. Between two DRAM nodes, ordinary NUMA balancing moves pages toward the CPU that uses them. The top-tier boundary separates the two cases (node_is_toptier()).

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Holt-Winters and ARIMA: models with trend and season
question: Which statement about ARIMA and exponential smoothing is correct according to FPP3?
options: SES is equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1), but multiplicative exponential smoothing models have no ARIMA equivalent
ARIMA strictly contains every exponential smoothing model
ARIMA cannot model seasonality
Exponential smoothing models are all stationary
explain: Linear (additive) ETS models map to ARIMA forms, for example ETS(A,N,N) to ARIMA(0,1,1). Nonlinear ETS models have no ARIMA counterpart, and all ETS models are nonstationary while some ARIMA models are stationary. Seasonal ARIMA handles seasonality with seasonal lags and differencing.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Why does CertificateVerify sign a hash of the whole transcript rather than just the server's key share?
options: Hashing makes the signature shorter
Certificates cannot sign raw key shares
The transcript includes the client's offers and both key shares, so any tampering with the negotiation makes the signature fail
It lets the server skip the Finished message
explain: Signing everything the client sent and received binds the server's identity to this exact negotiation. An attacker who removed strong options from the ClientHello would change the transcript, and the signature would not verify.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: Why can a man in the middle not simply erase the DOWNGRD sentinel from the ServerHello random?
options: The random is encrypted
The server random is covered by the server's signature (ServerKeyExchange in TLS 1.2), so changing it breaks the signature check
The sentinel is checked by the CA
The sentinel is repeated in every record
explain: The randoms are inputs to what the server signs in a TLS 1.2 (EC)DHE handshake. Altering any byte invalidates the signature, which the client verifies with the certificate's key.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
question: Why does ACME's key authorization include a thumbprint of the client's account key rather than just the token?
options: It binds the proof to one ACME account, so a different account cannot reuse someone else's published token to get authorized
To make the file larger
Because the CA cannot generate random tokens
To encrypt the token
explain: The CA checks that the published value matches the token AND the account requesting the order. Proof of control is tied to a specific requester.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
question: Why did Chrome remove HPKP?
options: Low adoption plus real risks: sites could lock out their own users, and attackers could set hostile pins; CT gave mis-issuance detection without those risks
Because it slowed down handshakes
Because CAs refused to support it
Because it only worked over HTTP/1.1
explain: Pinning's strength (hard rejection of unexpected keys) was also its danger. A mistake or a malicious pin could make a site unreachable for months.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Post-quantum key exchange: ML-KEM hybrids in TLS
question: A government agency records your TLS 1.3 traffic today, protected by plain X25519. Which threat does that create?
options: None, because TLS 1.3 has forward secrecy
A future quantum computer could solve X25519's discrete logarithm from the recorded key shares and decrypt the traffic (harvest now, decrypt later)
Only that your certificate could be forged today
Only metadata exposure
explain: Forward secrecy protects against later theft of long-term keys, not against breaking the ephemeral exchange itself. A quantum attacker breaks the recorded key shares directly, which is exactly what the hybrid prevents.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: A colleague removes other=0.0 from the A and B loads in the K loop because "the C store is masked anyway". When does this break?
options: Never, the store mask covers it
Only when M is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_M
When K is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_K, because undefined values in the last K tile get summed into every output
Only on AMD GPUs
explain: The store mask only drops rows and columns outside C. Garbage in the K dimension is not outside C: it is multiplied and accumulated into valid outputs. Masked K lanes must load 0.0, the neutral element of the sum in the dot product.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: Why can Transfusion open up attention inside the image when Chameleon cannot?
options: Transfusion uses a larger context window
Chameleon images are smaller
Transfusion denoises all patches of an image at once, so every patch exists at every step, whereas Chameleon emits patches one by one
Transfusion has no text tokens inside images
explain: In a diffusion step all n patches (noisy versions of them) are in the sequence simultaneously, so a patch attending to a later patch reads something real. In token-by-token generation a later patch has not been sampled yet, so letting an earlier one see it during training would be a leak.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
question: A unikernel serves files only from a RAM filesystem. Why does its image contain no block device driver, even though the Unikraft source tree has one?
options: The hypervisor provides block storage, so the driver is never needed
Block drivers are loaded as kernel modules at boot
Only components selected in the configuration or pulled in as dependencies are compiled and linked; nothing references the block layer
Dead code elimination removes all drivers by default
explain: Unikraft builds only selected micro-libraries and their dependencies. The paper notes the nginx image has no block subsystem because it only uses RamFS. There are no loadable modules in a unikernel.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: An attacker finds a buffer overflow in a C web server. On a Linux VM they get code execution as the unprivileged web server user. What changes if the same server runs as a unikernel without memory protections?
options: They get code execution with full control of the VM, including raw packet I/O, with no privilege escalation step needed
Nothing: the hypervisor stops the exploit before it runs
The exploit fails because unikernels have no shell to spawn
They can immediately read the memory of other VMs on the host
explain: With one address space and one privilege level, the application is the kernel. NCC Group showed arbitrary packet I/O right after compromise. The hypervisor still confines the attacker to that VM, so other tenants remain protected unless the hypervisor itself is broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
question: Index A stores 1,536-d fp32 vectors. Index B stores 768-d int8 vectors. On a memory-bound scan, roughly how many more distances per second can B compute?
options: About the same, since both do one distance per vector
2x, because B has half the dimensions
8x, because B reads 768 bytes per vector instead of 6,144
4x, because int8 is a quarter of fp32
explain: Bytes per vector set the ceiling. A reads 1,536 x 4 = 6,144 bytes, B reads 768 x 1 = 768 bytes, a ratio of 8. Half the dimensions and a quarter of the bytes per dimension multiply.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
question: A researcher wants to add a second, greedy generation pass per prompt (as ReMax does) to compute a baseline. In verl's design, what has to change?
options: Every worker's SPMD program, because each must know when the extra pass happens
Only the controller loop: one more call to the existing generate_sequences with sampling turned off
The NCCL communicator setup between actor and critic
Nothing: verl decides which passes to run from the model architecture
explain: Stages are named calls on WorkerGroups, so a new dataflow is a new sequence of calls in the controller. The HybridFlow paper shows PPO, ReMax and Safe-RLHF (which adds a cost model that scores harmfulness) differing only in these few lines. In a multi-controller design the extra pass would have to be threaded through every model's program.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Weight handoff: from 3D-HybridEngine to sleep, wake and streaming
question: You raise `update_weights_bucket_megabytes` from 512 to 4096 on a colocated run. What changes?
options: The rollout keeps two full copies of the weights during the handoff
The KV cache is restored before the weights
Fewer bucket round trips, at the cost of a larger transient buffer on every GPU during the handoff
Each tensor is cast to bf16 before sending
explain: The bucket is one reusable buffer: a bigger one means fewer metadata-and-acknowledge round trips but more GPU memory held while streaming. Nothing about the order of moves or the dtype changes, and no second copy of the model is ever built.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Agent loops: multi-turn rollouts and tool calling in verl
question: What does LLMServerClient's sticky session buy in a multi-turn rollout?
options: It guarantees the same random seed for every turn
Each turn of a session goes to the server that already holds its earlier tokens in the prefix cache, so the next turn's prefill is mostly reused
It lets two servers split one sequence's KV cache
It forces all sessions of a prompt onto one GPU so GRPO groups stay together
explain: The first turn picks the least-loaded server; later turns with the same request_id go back to it. Its prefix cache already holds the conversation, so only the new tokens need prefill. Group membership is tracked by uid, not by server.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions
question: A frame grid of 24 x 24 tokens is average-pooled with a 3 x 3 window. How many tokens remain per frame?
explain: 24 / 3 = 8 per side, so 8 x 8 = 64 tokens, a 9x reduction from 576. Pooling by k x k divides the count by k squared.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
question: Ha and Schmidhuber's VizDoom agent scored well inside its dream but poorly in the real game. What is the most likely cause?
options: The controller had too few parameters to play Doom
The VAE compressed frames to 32 numbers, which is too few to see anything
The policy exploited errors in the learned model that do not exist in the real game
Dreams always run at a different frame rate than the game
explain: The paper calls this cheating the world model: the controller finds an adversarial policy that triggers the model's mistakes. Making the dream noisier (higher temperature) made such exploits harder. Any agent trained inside a learned simulator can overfit to its flaws.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
question: You train two models on the same data. Model X has FVD 80 and delta PSNR 0.1; model Y has FVD 90 and delta PSNR 1.8. You want a playable environment. Which do you pick and why?
options: X, because lower FVD always means a better world model
Neither, FVD under 100 means both are unusable
Y, because X's actions barely change its output, so it is a good video model but a poor interactive one
X, because delta PSNR only matters for robotics
explain: A world model must respond to actions. X generates slightly more realistic clips but random actions make almost no difference to its output. Y trades a little fidelity for strong control, the same tradeoff Genie made when choosing a pixel-input LAM.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: I/O virtualization: emulation, virtio, passthrough and the IOMMU
question: Which I/O approach exposes the least host device-emulation code to a guest?
options: Full emulation of a legacy floppy controller
An assigned NVMe drive behind an IOMMU
A virtio block device
Emulated IDE
explain: With passthrough the device model is mostly gone; the guest talks to real hardware, and the IOMMU plus interrupt remapping enforce the boundary. The trade-offs are hardware cost, live migration and trusting the device's own firmware.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: VENOM, the floppy controller every guest had
question: Two Xen hosts are equally unpatched for VENOM. Host A runs HVM guests with the device model in dom0; host B uses qemu-dm stub domains. What does XSA-133 say about host B?
options: It is not vulnerable at all
It is more vulnerable, because stub domains share memory with dom0
It is vulnerable only to takeover of the stub (service) domain, not of dom0
Stub domains only help PV guests
explain: XSA-133: guests using a qemu-dm stubdomain 'are only vulnerable to takeover of that service domain'. The bug is unchanged; the privileges it yields are much smaller.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Side channels across VMs: what the hypervisor must flush and isolate
question: A KVM host flushes L1D unconditionally on every VM entry, keeps SMT on, and lets any vCPU run on any thread. Is VM A's L1TF exposure to host data closed?
options: Yes, the flush removes all host data before VM A runs
No: a sibling hyperthread running host code (or another VM) refills the shared L1D while VM A runs
Yes, because EPT blocks L1TF
No, because the flush is only conditional
explain: The kernel's L1TF document: 'L1D flush does not prevent the SMT problem because the sibling thread will also bring back its data into the L1D'. Unconditional mode does not change that; dedicated cores, core scheduling or nosmt do.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Turning an image into a sequence of patch tokens
question: You feed a 384x384 image to a ViT-B/16 (patch size stays 16). How long is the sequence the encoder processes?
options: 197, because the model was built for 224x224 and the extra pixels are cropped
577: a 24x24 grid of patches plus the CLS token
576: one token per patch, since the CLS token is only used at 224
1153, because the patch count scales with the image side length times 3 channels
explain: 384 / 16 = 24 patches per side, so 576 patches, plus CLS: 577. The transformer itself accepts any sequence length (up to memory); what does not fit is the table of 197 position embeddings, which is the subject of lesson 3.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: You train LoRA (r = 16 on query and value) for ViT-B/16 and then merge the adapters with W = W0 + (alpha/r)BA. Compared with the original model, the merged model at inference has:
options: The same parameter count and the same latency
About 590K more parameters and a slightly slower forward pass
Half the parameters, since A and B replace W0
Lower accuracy, because merging rounds the update to low rank
explain: Merging adds BA into the existing matrices, so shapes are unchanged and so is the forward cost. The LoRA paper stresses this property: no additional inference latency compared with a fully fine-tuned model. The update was low rank during training too, so merging loses nothing.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
question: In the toy, you replace the 10 Euler steps with a single step of size 1 from tau = 0. What chunk comes out of the noise sample (0.25, 0.10)?
options: (0.6, 0.8), the R mode
(-0.6, -0.8), the L mode
(0.25, 0.10), unchanged
(0, 0), the average of the modes
explain: At tau = 0 both weights are 0.5, so v = (mean of modes) - x and x + v is the mean, (0, 0). One big step reproduces the regression failure; several small steps let the weights sharpen before the chunk moves far.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: A new encoder output is z = (0.1, -2.2). Using the toy codebook, which token id does it get?
explain: Squared distances: e5 gives 0.01 + 0.64 = 0.65, e3 gives 0.81 + 1.44 = 2.25 and e2 gives 1.21 + 1.44 = 2.65. The far-away code e5 wins, and that is exactly how a dead code can come back to life: an encoder output has to land near it.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: Chameleon's paper says its tokenizer struggles to reconstruct images containing a lot of text. What does that imply for the full model?
options: Nothing, because the transformer can learn the missing detail from more data
Its performance on text-heavy, OCR-like image tasks is upper-bounded by what the tokenizer keeps
Its text-only benchmarks will suffer
It must switch to continuous image features for those inputs
explain: The transformer only ever sees the token ids. Detail lost at tokenization cannot be recovered downstream, so the tokenizer caps OCR-heavy performance, as the paper states.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: A model mixes a backend whose builder reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Is the batch sorted decodes first?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes: the runner sorts every batch decode-first whatever the thresholds say; the threshold only tells each builder where its decodes end
Only on steps that contain no prefills
explain: On main, sort_batch_req_ids in the GPU model runner orders every batch, and one order is shared by all layers. reorder_batch_threshold is read only by builders, which pass it to split_decodes_and_prefills as the decode cutoff. Backends with one varlen kernel, such as FLASH_ATTN, accept any order.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
question: With `max_num_seqs = 256` (max capture size 512), which batch wastes the largest *fraction* of its padded graph?
options: 257 tokens
100 tokens
9 tokens
511 tokens
explain: 9 pads to 16, wasting 7 of 16 rows (43.8%). 257 pads to 272 (5.5%), 100 to 104 (3.8%) and 511 to 512 (0.2%). Small batches matter most for latency, which is why `performance_mode = interactivity` captures every size from 1 to 32.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
question: You must read 6 pt text on scanned invoices with an OpenAI model that uses the tile rule. Which choice best protects accuracy?
options: Set detail to low to save tokens
Send the full 4000 px scan and trust the model
Crop the text region (or split the page) so that after the 768 px shortest-side rule the text stays legible
Convert the image to grayscale
explain: With the tile rule a big page is shrunk until its shortest side is 768 px, which can make small print illegible. Low detail is even coarser. Cropping or splitting keeps more pixels per character.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
question: Thread 1's enqueue was linearized by a helper, but a different helper is still suspended between marking thread 1 not pending and swinging tail. Thread 1 returns immediately and starts a new operation. What does the paper say goes wrong if `enq()` skips its final `help_finish_enq()` call?
options: Nothing, because tail is only a hint
The node is enqueued twice
Thread 1's next dequeue returns the wrong value
Further enqueues can be blocked until the suspended helper resumes, which breaks wait-freedom
explain: help_finish_enq checks that the owner's descriptor still points at the dangling node. Once thread 1 has published a new descriptor that check fails, so no one fixes tail and every later enqueue waits on the suspended helper. The final call ensures tail is past your node before you return.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
question: A team trains a 6-hour model only on single-step targets and finds its 10-day rollouts drift badly. Which fix is GraphCast's approach?
options: Train on 1-hour steps so each step is easier
Add more layers so the single-step error goes to zero
Use an L1 loss instead of MSE
Backpropagate a loss over several autoregressive steps, growing the number of steps during training
explain: GraphCast's loss covers N rollout steps, increased from 1 to 12, so the model sees its own outputs as inputs during training. Shorter steps mean more calls and more accumulated error (Pangu's finding), and no network reaches zero one-step error.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
question: You find a bug on a site with a published VDP but no bounty. What does the VDP give you that a site with no policy does not?
options: A stated permission to test within its rules and a way to report
Payment for valid reports
Permission to test every system the company owns
The right to publish immediately
explain: A VDP states what testing is allowed and how to report, and usually promises not to pursue good-faith reporters. It does not pay (that is a bounty), does not extend beyond its listed scope, and normally asks for time before publication.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Recon at bounty scale: wildcards, subdomains and live hosts
question: A policy lists `*.shop.example` in scope. Your recon finds `shop.example` (the bare domain). What should you do?
options: Check whether the policy lists the apex separately, and ask the programme if it is unclear
Test it; the wildcard obviously includes it
Test it only with automated tools
Report it as out of scope
explain: A wildcard covers subdomains; the apex is a different name. Many policies list it explicitly, some do not. When the written scope is ambiguous, ask before testing.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authorization at scale: two accounts and a replay matrix
question: Your replay shows that your second test account can read your first account's invoices by changing the id. What is the strongest evidence to include in the report?
options: The two requests and responses using only your own two accounts, with ids and timestamps
Ten other customers' invoices to show the scale
A script that downloads all invoices
The number of customers on the platform
explain: Your own two accounts prove the missing check completely. Pulling other customers' data adds nothing to the proof, violates the programme rules and may itself be a breach.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Reading a programme policy: scope, rules and safe harbour
question: A shop's policy has a strong safe-harbour clause. During testing you find its checkout calls a payment provider's API. Does the shop's safe harbour cover testing that API?
options: No; safe harbour covers only claims the shop controls, so the provider's own policy decides
Yes, because it is part of the checkout
Yes, if you use your own account
Only if the bug is critical
explain: The disclose.io template says safe harbour applies only to legal claims under the participating organisation's control and does not bind independent third parties. The payment provider must authorise testing of its own systems.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: How a page loads: HTML, subresources, JavaScript and the DOM
question: A page has, in order: `
options: a.js, because a plain script tag blocks parsing
Only b.png, because images are large
c.js, because async means the parser waits for it
None of them; browsers never pause parsing
explain: A script tag without async or defer stops the parser until the script is fetched and executed. Images are fetched in parallel, and async scripts run whenever they arrive without blocking the parser.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
question: Which of these Set-Cookie headers, sent by https://shop.example.com, will a supporting browser reject?
options: `__Secure-sid=1; Secure; Domain=example.com`
`__Host-sid=1; Secure; Path=/; Domain=example.com`
`__Host-sid=1; Secure; Path=/`
`sid=1; Secure; HttpOnly`
explain: A __Host- cookie must have Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute. The first one sets Domain, so it is rejected. __Secure- only requires Secure from an HTTPS page, so Domain is allowed there.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
question: Why must a CSP nonce be different on every response?
options: A fixed nonce can be learned once and then copied into injected script tags, defeating the policy
Nonces expire after 60 seconds
HTTP/2 requires unique header values
Browsers cache nonces and refuse repeats
explain: The nonce works only because the attacker cannot predict it. If it is the same on every response, an attacker reads it from any page view and adds nonce="..." to their injected tag, which the browser will then run.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Subresource Integrity and the trust you hand to third-party scripts
question: Why does an SRI-protected cross-origin script need `crossorigin="anonymous"` and an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header?
options: To send the user's cookies to the CDN
To encrypt the file in transit
Integrity checks are only allowed on CORS fetches; in no-cors mode they would let pages probe the content of other sites' private files
Because SHA-384 requires a CORS header
explain: If integrity worked in no-cors mode, an attacker's page could request a private resource with a guessed hash and learn from success or failure whether the guess was right. Requiring CORS means the server has agreed the content may be read anyway.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
question: Why does PowerShell filtering use `Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'` rather than searching the text of each line?
options: Because the pipeline carries objects with named properties, so you compare a property directly
Because PowerShell has no text search
Because Status is a keyword of the shell
Because Where-Object only works on services
explain: Cmdlets emit .NET objects. Each has properties you can compare, sort and select, which is more reliable than matching text that might change format.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: NTFS permissions and inheritance: reading and fixing an ACL
question: A folder shows `CONTOSO\Sales:(I)(OI)(CI)(M)`. An admin runs `icacls` on that folder to remove Sales and it reports success, but Sales still has access. What is the most likely reason?
options: The ACE is inherited (I) from a parent folder, so it must be changed on the parent or inheritance broken here
icacls cannot remove groups
Sales is a built-in group that cannot be removed
The change applies only after a reboot
explain: (I) means the ACE was inherited. Removing explicit ACEs here does not touch it. Change the parent folder's ACL, or disable inheritance on this folder.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event logs: anatomy of a record, and reading logons (4624, 4625)
question: A file server logs many 4625 events with Sub Status 0xC0000064 from one IP address, each for a different name. What is most likely happening?
options: Someone is trying user names that do not exist, enumerating accounts
An admin mistyped a password
A disabled account is in use
The server's clock is wrong
explain: 0xC0000064 means the user name does not exist. Many of them in a row is a sign of user enumeration, often followed by password guessing on the names that work.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
question: Why could WannaCry spread inside a network with nobody opening an email?
options: It was a worm: it scanned for SMB on TCP 445 and exploited unpatched SMBv1 servers directly
It guessed user passwords over RDP
It used a UAC bypass
It was installed by Windows Update
explain: The EternalBlue exploit needs only network access to a vulnerable SMBv1 server. No user action is required on the target, which is what makes it wormable.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why wireless is different: a medium anyone in range can hear
question: Why can't a wireless intrusion detection system alert on someone quietly recording your Wi-Fi traffic?
options: Because a passive receiver transmits nothing, so there is no signal to detect
It can: every receiver sends an acknowledgement
Because recording requires joining the network first
Because monitor mode is illegal
explain: NIST SP 800-153 makes this point: passive attacks only intercept radio transmissions, so there is nothing to monitor. Defences against eavesdropping are cryptographic, not detective.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2-Enterprise: 802.1X, EAP and the certificate check that matters
question: Which two client settings together implement SP 800-97's advice for EAP server validation in wpa_supplicant?
options: identity and password
eap=MD5 and phase2
ssid and psk
ca_cert pointing to the company CA, and domain_match (or domain_suffix_match) naming the RADIUS server
explain: ca_cert limits trust to your CA; domain_match checks the certificate's name. Either alone leaves a gap: a CA alone accepts any certificate that CA issued, a name alone accepts any CA.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
question: A user on hotel Wi-Fi types `bank.example` (no https://) into a browser that has never visited it, and the site is not on the HSTS preload list. Where is the risk?
options: The first request goes out as plain HTTP, so a hostile network can answer it and keep the user on an attacker-controlled HTTP page
Only the DNS lookup is exposed
The bank's certificate will be stolen
None; the bank uses HTTPS
explain: This is RFC 6797's bootstrap MITM problem: HSTS only helps after the browser has seen the header over HTTPS, or if the site is preloaded. Preloading moves the protection to the very first visit.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: App permissions and the principle of least privilege
question: A to-do list app requests location, contacts and microphone at first launch, before showing any screen. Which least-privilege principle does this violate most directly?
options: Request permissions late, tied to the specific user action that needs them, and only those a feature actually uses
All permissions must be install-time
Apps must use signature permissions
Apps must not use the internet
explain: Android's guidance is to request runtime permissions as late as possible, in context, and to request the minimum. A to-do list has no obvious need for any of these at launch, which is also a red flag in app review.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Zero-click attacks: from Trident to the Pixel 9 chain
question: Why did the Pixel 9 chain need only two bugs while iPhone zero-click chains like Triangulation needed four or more?
options: Two-bug chains are impossible on iOS
The Pixel used WEP
Android has no sandbox
On the Pixel 9 the decoder's sandbox could reach a vulnerable driver directly and lacked the AOSP seccomp policy, so one escape bug reached the kernel
explain: Project Zero's part 3: few bugs were needed because the mediacodec context could reach the BigWave driver and the expected seccomp policy was missing. Longer chains are a sign of effective sandboxing; their recommendation was to reduce what media processes can reach.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS
question: A thief's steal returns ABORT. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Another thread won the CAS on top; the deque may still hold tasks, so retry or try elsewhere
The victim's deque is empty, so stop trying it
The deque is corrupted and must be reset
The owner is resizing, so the thief must wait on a lock
explain: ABORT (Retry in crossbeam) only means this thief lost a race on top, against another thief or the owner taking the last task. Treating it as empty can make a worker park while work remains.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
question: A teammate evaluates the 50% checkpoint of a cosine run (T = S) and concludes that 'training on half the data gives loss X'. Why is X misleading?
options: The checkpoint has seen only half the data, so X is accurate by definition
The LR at that point is still about 0.55 of peak, so the model has not been annealed; a run with T equal to half the length would reach a lower loss
Cosine checkpoints are always better than fully trained models of the same length, so X is too optimistic
Weight decay has not taken effect yet at 50% of training
explain: Mid-run cosine checkpoints are underestimates. Most of the loss drop from annealing happens when the LR gets small, which for this run only happens near S. A cosine run with T set to the shorter length would anneal earlier and end lower.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Run it yourself: one stable trunk, three cooldown branches
question: Spot the bug: a branch for a 6,000-step model starts at step 4,800 and calls `run(m, opt, gen, 4800, 6000, lambda t: wsd(t, 4800, 6000))`. What happens?
options: Nothing: the decay length only matters for linear cooldowns
The cooldown is spread over 6,000 steps, so at step 6,000 the LR is still 1 - sqrt(0.2), about 0.55 of peak, and the model never anneals
The LR drops to zero immediately at step 4,800
The branch reruns warmup
explain: decay_len must be total - start = 1,200. With 6,000, the run stops when p = 1,200 / 6,000 = 0.2 of the way through the decay, at 1 - sqrt(0.2) = 0.553 of the peak: a half-annealed model, the same problem as stopping cosine early.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
question: sendfile(sock, fd, &pos, 3221225472) on a blocking socket returns 2147479552. What should the code do?
options: Treat it as an error and close the connection
Reset pos to 0 and retry the whole file
Switch to read and write for the rest of the file
Call sendfile again with the remaining 1073745920 bytes; pos was already advanced
explain: A short count is normal: one call moves at most 0x7ffff000 bytes, and a socket can also accept less. Because a non-NULL offset pointer is updated by the kernel, the loop just calls again with what is left.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?
question: You run the NLI pipeline on 1,000 tickets with 50 candidate labels. How many NLI forward passes (one per sequence pair) does that take?
options: 50, one per label, cached across tickets
1,000, one per ticket
explain: The cross-encoder needs the premise and hypothesis together, so every (ticket, label) pair is its own forward pass: 1,000 x 50 = 50,000. Nothing about a label can be cached, because its representation depends on the ticket. This is the main cost of the NLI approach and grows linearly with the number of labels.
